analogy.p: Imagine driving to a friend's house. The distance is what the car's odometer records as you follow the winding roads, round roundabouts and down one-way streets. The displacement is how far away the house is 'as the crow flies', plus which compass direction the crow would fly. Speed is what the speedometer shows; velocity is that same reading plus the compass direction you are heading. If you drive round and round a roundabout, the speedometer needle never moves (constant speed) yet your direction keeps changing, so your velocity changes. The analogy breaks down because a real crow is not constrained by roads whereas displacement is purely a mathematical straight line, and the odometer-speedometer picture does not show the sign convention needed for vectors.

bullets: **Scalar** = magnitude (size) only, e.g. distance, speed, mass, time, energy, temperature.
**Vector** = magnitude AND direction, e.g. displacement, velocity, force, acceleration, momentum.
Directions can be given in words (north, up, to the right), as a bearing, or by sign: positive one way and negative the other along a straight line.
A negative sign on a vector only tells you the direction is opposite to the one you chose as positive. It does not make the size 'smaller'.
Scalars add like ordinary numbers; vectors must take direction into account (3 km east then 3 km west gives a displacement of zero, not 6 km).
In diagrams vectors are drawn as arrows: the length shows the magnitude and the arrowhead shows the direction.
Link: the same scalar/vector split reappears in forces (resultant force) and momentum later in the Forces topic.
core.h: Scalar and vector quantities: the idea behind this whole topic
core.p: Every quantity in motion is either a **scalar** (it has size, also called magnitude, only) or a **vector** (it has size AND a direction). The specification pairs them up: **distance** is the scalar and **displacement** is its vector partner; **speed** is the scalar and **velocity** is its vector partner. Keeping these pairs straight is the key to every question in this topic. A vector needs a direction to be a complete answer, so a vector quantity written without direction (for example 'displacement = 5 km') earns fewer marks than one written with it ('5 km north-east').

bullets: Distance = the total length of the path travelled; it does not care about direction changes or turns.
Distance is always zero or positive; it can never be negative.
Walking round a 400 m running track once gives a distance of 400 m, however many bends there are.
Odometer readings in a car measure distance (they keep adding up), not displacement.
A longer route between the same two places means a greater distance.
Units: metre (m); also km (1 km = 1000 m), cm, mm. Always convert to metres before using v in m/s.
Exam tip: when a question says 'how far', 'total distance' or 'length of the route', give a single positive number with units and no direction.
core.p: **Distance** is how far an object moves. It is a **scalar quantity**: it has a size but no direction. Distance depends on the actual route taken and is measured along the path, so it can only ever increase (or stay the same) as an object keeps moving. It is measured in metres (m) in the SI system, although kilometres (km) are common for journeys.

bullets: Displacement = straight-line distance from start to finish PLUS the direction of that line.
Displacement is never larger than the distance travelled; the two are equal only for motion in a straight line without turning back.
A complete round trip returns the object to its start, so the displacement is **zero** even though the distance may be large.
In a straight-line problem choose a positive direction (e.g. right = +). Moving left then gives negative displacement.
When motion is in two directions at right angles, find the size of the displacement with Pythagoras and the direction with trigonometry (Higher tier style question).
Displacement is shown on diagrams as an arrow drawn directly from the start point to the finish point.
Common context: an athlete running a 400 m lap has covered a distance of 400 m but ends with displacement 0 m.
core.p: **Displacement** includes both the distance an object moves, measured in a **straight line from the start point to the finish point**, and the **direction** of that straight line. It is a **vector quantity**. Displacement is concerned only with where you end up relative to where you started, not with the path you took to get there. Because of that, displacement can be smaller than distance, can be zero, and can be negative if a direction has been chosen as positive.

bullets: Two-leg walk, 3 km east then 4 km north: distance 7 km (scalar), displacement 5 km on a bearing of about 037 (vector).
Walking 100 m east then 100 m west: distance 200 m, displacement 0 m.
Swimming 5 lengths of a 25 m pool starting at one end: distance 125 m; you finish at the opposite end so displacement is 25 m in the direction of the lengths.
A ball thrown straight up 10 m and caught at the same height: distance 20 m, displacement 0 m.
A car driven round a roundabout and leaving at the far side: the distance along the curve is longer than the straight-line displacement.
Exam checking trick: if your calculated displacement is bigger than the distance, you have made an error.
Command word 'calculate the displacement' usually wants size AND direction for full marks.
core.p: The best way to understand the difference is to compare the same journey measured both ways. If you walk 3 km east and then 4 km north, you have travelled a total distance of 3 + 4 = 7 km. Your displacement is the straight line from where you started to where you finished. The two legs are at right angles so Pythagoras applies: displacement = square root of (3 squared + 4 squared) = square root of 25 = 5 km. The direction is found with trigonometry: the angle from north is tan inverse of (3 divided by 4) = 37 degrees, so the displacement is 5 km on a bearing of about 037 degrees.

bullets: Equation: distance (m) = speed (m/s) x time (s), or s = v t.
Rearrangements: speed = distance / time; time = distance / speed.
Use the triangle: put s on top and v, t on the bottom. Cover the quantity you want.
Units must be consistent: metres, seconds and m/s together. Convert minutes to seconds (x 60) and km to m (x 1000) first.
To convert km/h to m/s divide by 3.6 (e.g. 72 km/h = 20 m/s); to convert m/s to km/h multiply by 3.6.
The equation applies to constant speed. For changing speed it gives the **average speed**: average speed = total distance / total time.
Sanity check: if a person walks at 1.5 m/s, a 3 km journey takes 3000 / 1.5 = 2000 s, about 33 minutes. Does your answer look sensible?
core.h: Speed and the equation distance = speed x time
core.p: **Speed** is how fast an object is moving, regardless of direction, so it is a **scalar quantity**. For an object moving at **constant speed**, the distance travelled in a given time is calculated using **distance travelled (m) = speed (m/s) x time (s)**, written s = v t. This is a recall equation: you must learn it, and be able to rearrange it to v = s / t and t = s / v. The unit of speed in physics is metres per second (m/s), which means 'metres travelled every second'.

bullets: Walking: about **1.5 m/s**.
Running: about **3 m/s**.
Cycling: about **6 m/s**.
A car on a motorway: roughly 30 m/s (about 70 mph); in a town about 13 m/s (about 30 mph). These are approximate.
Sound in air: about **330 m/s**.
Wind speed varies widely, from nearly 0 on a still day to over 30 m/s in a storm. Wind speed is not a fixed value.
The speed of sound also varies: it depends on the temperature and the material it travels through, and is much faster in solids and liquids than in air.
Use these values in estimate questions, e.g. 'estimate the time to cycle 3 km': 3000 / 6 = 500 s, a little over 8 minutes.
core.p: The specification expects you to recall typical values for everyday speeds so you can judge whether an answer is sensible or estimate times and distances. These are approximate because the speed of a moving object is rarely constant. Walking and running speeds depend on the person's fitness, age and terrain, and a bicycle's speed depends on effort and slope.

bullets: Average speed = total distance travelled / total time taken (including any stops).
Instantaneous speed = speed at one moment in time, e.g. the reading on a speedometer.
A journey with stops has a lower average speed than the speed while moving.
Speed of wind and speed of sound also change with conditions; changes in speed are not just for moving vehicles.
Example: 90 km in 1.5 hours gives an average speed of 60 km/h, even if parts of the journey were faster or slower.
Average speed is NOT the average of two speeds unless the times spent at each speed are equal. Always use total distance divided by total time.
Link: how quickly speed changes is the acceleration (next point).
core.h: Speed is rarely constant: average and instantaneous speed
core.p: The specification says that the speed of a moving object is rarely constant. When walking, running or travelling in a car, the speed is constantly changing: you speed up, slow down and stop. The equation s = v t is therefore normally used with an **average speed** over the journey. The speed at a particular moment is called the **instantaneous speed**, which is what a car's speedometer shows. On a distance-time graph the instantaneous speed is the gradient at that point.

bullets: Velocity = speed in a stated direction, e.g. 12 m/s east.
Average velocity = displacement / time taken (note: displacement, not distance).
On a straight line with a chosen positive direction, velocity is positive one way and negative the other.
A runner completing a lap has average speed 8 m/s (400 m in 50 s) but average velocity 0 m/s, because the displacement is zero.
Same speed, different direction means different velocity.
Velocity is the vector partner of speed, just as displacement is the vector partner of distance.
On a velocity-time graph a negative velocity means moving in the opposite direction to the positive one.
core.p: **Velocity** is the speed of an object in a given direction. It is a **vector quantity**. Two objects can therefore have the same speed but different velocities if they are heading in different directions. A car travelling at 20 m/s north and another at 20 m/s south have the same speed but opposite velocities (+20 m/s and -20 m/s if north is chosen as positive). Velocity can change when the speed changes, when the direction changes, or both.

bullets: At any point the velocity points along the tangent to the circle, at right angles to the radius.
Examples: a car going round a roundabout at constant speed, the Moon orbiting the Earth, a satellite in a circular orbit, a stone whirled on a string, a person on a fairground wheel.
Speed is constant: the size of the velocity vector does not change.
Velocity changes: the direction of the velocity vector keeps changing.
Because velocity changes, there is acceleration; this needs a resultant force acting towards the centre (e.g. gravity for the Moon, tension in the string, friction between tyres and road).
Model answer: 'The speed is constant but the direction is changing, so the velocity (a vector) is changing.'
Do not say velocity is constant just because speed is constant. This is the commonest error on this topic.
core.h: Constant speed but changing velocity: circular motion
core.p: The specification requires you to explain qualitatively, with examples, that **motion in a circle involves constant speed but changing velocity**. An object going round a circle at steady speed covers equal distances in equal times, so its speed does not change. However, its direction of motion is continually changing, and since velocity is a vector with direction included, the velocity is changing all the time. A changing velocity means the object is **accelerating**, even though the speed is constant, and a resultant force (the centripetal force) must act towards the centre of the circle.

bullets: Method: mark a start line and finish line a measured distance apart (use a metre rule or tape measure to the nearest mm or cm).
Time the object between the lines with a stopwatch and repeat several times, then calculate a mean time to reduce random error.
Calculate speed = distance / time.
Light gates connected to a data logger remove human reaction time and give much more accurate times; a card of known length on a trolley gives speed as card length / time to pass the gate.
Use a longer distance to reduce the percentage error caused by reaction time.
Possible sources of error: parallax when reading the ruler, reaction time at start and end, friction or air resistance changing the speed along the track.
Control variables for comparing speeds: same start position, same distance, same surface, same starting push or ramp height.
core.p: The specification asks you to be able to make measurements of distance and time and calculate speeds, using objects such as trolleys and ball bearings or an everyday moving object. The idea is always the same: measure a distance with a ruler, metre rule or tape measure, measure the time to cover it, then divide. Accuracy depends on how well you can measure the time, since human reaction time of about 0.2 s introduces a **random error** when using a stopwatch.

bullets: Step 1: list the data with units. Step 2: convert units (minutes to seconds, km to m). Step 3: write the equation. Step 4: rearrange if needed. Step 5: substitute. Step 6: answer with unit.
Distance and speed are scalars; displacement and velocity are vectors and need directions.
Average velocity = displacement / time and average speed = total distance / total time, so they can differ greatly.
Distance-time graphs (a later point): the gradient is the speed; velocity-time graphs show direction as positive or negative.
Acceleration (next point) is the rate of change of velocity, so circular motion at constant speed involves acceleration.
Higher tier extension: resolving a two-direction journey into a resultant displacement uses Pythagoras and trigonometry from maths (SOH CAH TOA).
Answers should be given to a suitable number of significant figures, matching the data (usually 2 or 3).
core.h: Pulling it together: strategy, units and links
core.p: For any motion calculation, follow the same strategy: identify whether the quantity is a scalar or vector, write the equation, convert to standard units, substitute, calculate, and give units (plus direction for vectors). The meaning of 'speed' and 'velocity' is tested both in short definitions and in calculations, so make sure you use the right word in your answer.

exam: Command words: 'State' (1 mark, recall); 'Calculate' (substitute and give a unit); 'Explain' (give a reason using linked statements); 'Describe' (what happens).
Definition marks: 'Distance is how far an object moves (scalar)'; 'Displacement is the straight-line distance from start to finish in a given direction (vector)'.
A 2-mark 'difference between speed and velocity' answer: 'Speed is scalar / has no direction (1); velocity is a vector / speed in a given direction (1)'.
Calculation marks usually: correct equation or rearrangement (1), substitution with correct units (1), answer (1), unit (1). Show every step even if you use a calculator.
Always convert units first. A very common lost mark is leaving time in minutes or distance in km while the answer is required in m/s.
For 'explain why velocity changes at constant speed' use: 'direction is changing (1); velocity is a vector so it changes if direction changes (1)'.

In 4 to 6 mark 'describe an experiment to measure speed' answers include: apparatus (ruler/tape, stopwatch or light gates), measure distance, measure time, repeat and average, calculate speed = distance / time, and one improvement (light gates).
Check sensible values: walking 1.5 m/s, running 3 m/s, cycling 6 m/s. A cyclist at 60 m/s means you have gone wrong somewhere.
Higher tier: displacement from two perpendicular legs needs Pythagoras for size and tan inverse for angle; state the direction in the answer.
Give answers to 2 or 3 significant figures and include the correct unit (m, m/s, s). Marks are routinely lost for missing or wrong units.

mistakes.r: Distance is a scalar (path length); displacement is a vector (straight-line start to finish, with direction).
mistakes.w: Displacement and distance are the same thing.

mistakes.r: Displacement is zero because start and finish are the same point; the distance is 400 m.
mistakes.w: A runner who finishes a lap has a displacement of 400 m.

mistakes.r: Velocity is a vector, so the changing direction means the velocity changes, even though speed is constant.
mistakes.w: An object moving in a circle at constant speed has constant velocity.

mistakes.r: Speed = distance / time; distance = speed x time.
Convert to metres and seconds first (or keep km and hours consistently).
mistakes.w: Using minutes or km straight in the m/s equation.

mistakes.r: Average speed = total distance / total time.
mistakes.w: Average speed is the mean of the start and end speeds.

mistakes.r: Vectors need a direction (e.g. 5 m/s north, or a +/- sign).
mistakes.w: Giving a velocity or displacement with no direction.

mistakes.r: The speed of sound varies with the medium and conditions (about 330 m/s in air).
mistakes.w: Speed of sound is the same everywhere.

mistakes.r: Walking is about 1.5 m/s; running about 3 m/s; cycling about 6 m/s.

summary: The specification asks you to know that distance is a scalar (how far an object moves) while displacement is a vector (straight-line start to finish with direction), and likewise that speed is a scalar and velocity is speed in a given direction. You must use distance = speed x time, recall typical speeds, explain that circular motion has constant speed but changing velocity, and measure speed in practicals. These ideas underpin acceleration, graphs, forces and momentum.

terms.d: A quantity that has magnitude (size) only and no direction.
A quantity that has both magnitude (size) and direction.
How far an object moves; a scalar quantity, measured along the path travelled.
The straight-line distance from the start point to the finish point together with the direction of that line; a vector quantity.
How fast an object is moving, without regard to direction; a scalar quantity measured in m/s.
The speed of an object in a given direction; a vector quantity.
Total distance travelled divided by total time taken.
The speed of an object at a particular moment in time.
Speed that does not change, so equal distances are covered in equal times.
The SI unit of speed and velocity: the distance in metres travelled in each second.
A direction given as an angle measured clockwise from north, written with three digits.
A straight line that touches a circle at one point; the velocity of a body moving in a circle points along it.
Motion along a circular path, with constant speed but continually changing velocity.
The single displacement that has the same effect as two or more separate displacements combined.
The time between a stimulus and a response, typically about 0.2 s, a source of error when timing by hand.

worked.q: A cyclist travels at a constant speed of 6.0 m/s for 5.0 minutes. Calculate the distance travelled. [3 marks]
steps: Convert time: 5.0 minutes x 60 = 300 s (1 mark).
Equation: s = v x t (1 mark).

worked.ans: (a) 7.0 km; (b) 5.0 km on a bearing of 037; (c) average speed 3.5 km/h, average velocity 2.5 km/h on a bearing of 037
worked.q: A student walks 3.0 km east and then 4.0 km north in a total time of 2.0 hours. (a) State the total distance. (b) Calculate the magnitude of the displacement. (c) Calculate the average speed in km/h and the magnitude of the average velocity. [6 marks]
steps: (b) The legs are at right angles so displacement = square root of (3.0 squared + 4.0 squared) (1 mark) = square root of 25 = 5.0 km (1 mark). Direction: tan inverse (3/4) = 37 degrees east of north, bearing 037 (1 mark).
(c) Average speed = total distance / total time = 7.0 / 2.0 = 3.5 km/h (1 mark). Average velocity = displacement / time = 5.0 / 2.0 = 2.5 km/h in the direction 037 (1 mark).

worked.ans: Average speed 8.0 m/s but average velocity 0 m/s, because velocity uses displacement (a vector) which is zero for a full lap.
worked.q: A runner completes one lap of a 400 m track in 50 s. Explain, using calculations, why her average speed is different from her average velocity. [4 marks]
steps: Average speed = distance / time = 400 / 50 = 8.0 m/s (1 mark).
After one lap she is back at the start, so her displacement is 0 m (1 mark).
Average velocity = displacement / time = 0 / 50 = 0 m/s (1 mark).
Speed is a scalar, which depends on the total path length, but velocity is a vector which depends on displacement; since the displacement is zero the velocity is zero (1 mark).
